newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch pension funds head for EMU by way of Germany.
newsitem.headline: Dutch pension funds head for EMU by way of Germany.

text.p: Facing a sharp drop in government bond issuance at home and seeking a broader spread of investments en route to EMU, some Dutch pension funds have been raising Germany's weighting in their fixed-income portfolios.
Mario Hooghiemstra, head of fixed income at steel maker Hoogovens' pension fund, said his limit for German mark bonds was raised to eight percent from four percent late last year.
"We have taken the first steps to allocate more to Germany," Hooghiemstra said.
The higher limit for marks, he said, was a response to the drop in Dutch government bond issues and an accompanying narrowing of the yield spreads offered by other guilder issuers.
"The Dutch curve is expensive relative to Germany and that is largely explained by the lack of paper around," he said.
In 1995 the government issued 53 billion guilders' worth of bonds, but last year the total fell to 33 billion guilders as the deficit was slashed to meet EMU qualification targets.
Details of this year's bond issuance are sketchy but most dealers, analysts and fund managers expect another sharp fall.
Reduced supply has driven up prices and brought down yields which dipped below those of German government bonds ("bunds") in the first quarter of last year and have stayed there ever since.
Scarcity of Dutch government bonds has also led to smaller yield pick-ups on non-government issues such as those issued by the Bank Nederlandse Gemeenten (BNG).
But fund managers said German bonds offered a good alternative to guilder bonds because of the very limited exchange rate risk involved for Dutch investors.
Since 1983 the Dutch central bank has kept the guilder at a virtually constant exchange rate of 1.12 marks.

Roelie van Wijk, fixed income manager at electronics group Philips' pension fund, said her fund had stopped distinguishing between guilder and mark bonds in 1996. Previously a minimum 75 percent of fixed-income assets had to be invested in guilders, but this level now applies jointly to both currencies.
Van Wijk said Dutch institutions would probably invest increasingly in German mark bonds as the likely conversion rates of the guilder and the mark into euros became clearer.
"If the Dutch-German yield spread is still a pick-up for Germany and you're not hampered by restrictions then I would see no reason not to invest more in Germany," she said.

At the end of 1995 the Philips fund had total assets of 24.1 billion guilders, of which just under half was invested in fixed income instruments. Some 10 percent of the fixed-income portfolio was invested in marks both then and the end of 1996.
Van Wijk said Dutch government bonds accounted for more than 50 percent of her fund's investment in guilder debt.

But reduced government issuance had not caused her any problems, she said, adding that she was just as happy to invest in other highly rated guilder borrowers, such as the BNG or in mark-denominated bonds.

Hooghiemstra said the Hoogovens fund -- with total assets of 6.2 billion guilders at the end of 1995 -- currently had some 60 percent of its money in fixed-income assets and that this was unlikely to change much as it was a relatively "mature" fund.
Hooghiemstra said he expected to raise his mark investments gradually towards the new eight percent limit this year.

Most money would go into bunds but some would also be allocated to other types of issue such as Pfandbriefe, asset-backed bonds issued by German banks, he said. Guilder debt will fall to around 88 percent of the fixed-income portfolio from 92 while other non-guilder debt will stay at around four.

Paul Vermaas of the health workers' pension fund PGGM agreed that reduced supply and undiminished domestic demand had driven down Dutch bond yields and prompted many funds to look more and more at Germany and other likely first-wave EMU candidates.
But as head of fixed income, Vermaas has been a net seller as PGGM plans to raise equities to 50-60 percent of all assets.
PGGM had total assets of 56.9 billion guilders at the end of 1995, with equities rising to 40 percent of the portfolio from 20 in 1991 while fixed income fell to 47 percent from 63.
"The lack of new (government) paper hasn't affected us much. In fact it has helped us sell at favourable terms," he said.
Vermaas is currently limited to a 20 percent maximum for non-guilder investments while some 50 percent of his guilder portfolio is invested in Dutch government debt.
PGGM is already planning for the advent of EMU and in fixed income this will mean diversification away from Dutch borrowers and more non-government foreign issuers entering the portfolio.
"Good corporate names are certainly eligible...but we won't be looking for non-investment grade bonds," he said.
Hooghiemstra at Hoogovens said he was also looking forward to the broader opportunities available once the single currency was launched and with it a single European bond market.
"It will become much more attractive and more interesting for portfolio managers...we will be operating in a wider market with greater freedom of movement," he said.
